title: Celestial Axis Measurement — Frames, Unit Vectors, Angular Separation, Precession and Toroidal Geometry
status: astronomical measurement framework + project-claim audit; not theological validation
abstract: North/Sirius/Regulus/Galactic-Center/torus language becomes scientifically tractable only after a reference frame, epoch, observer, target vector and uncertainty are declared. This paper supplies the coordinate machinery required to test directional claims rather than relying on visual diagrams or numerical resemblance. Celestial objects are represented as unit vectors derived from right ascension and declination; alignments are quantified by great-circle angular separation; local pointing adds observer latitude/longitude and sidereal time; epoch changes are handled through standard precession/proper-motion transformations. The same discipline clarifies the remembered torus calculation: a torus has at least two independent radii, so one remembered circumference-like number cannot uniquely reconstruct its geometry. The project can therefore preserve symbolic North/Axis material while giving astronomical claims a reproducible measurement contract.
epistemic_rule: Astronomical coordinates test physical sky geometry only. They cannot test whether North, Sirius, Regulus or any star carries a theological office. Symbolic/project mappings remain distinct even when an astronomical alignment is measured accurately.

required_fields: observer position if local horizon coordinates are used
observation time if local pointing is used
measurement_contract.rule: The phrase 'points to' is incomplete until these fields determine a physical vector comparison.

equatorial_unit_vector.input: right ascension alpha and declination delta in a declared frame such as ICRS
equatorial_unit_vector.units: alpha,delta in radians inside trigonometric functions; n dimensionless and unit norm
equatorial_unit_vector.use: Converts named sky positions into ordinary vector geometry.

angular_separation.numerical_note: For production calculations use a numerically stable great-circle routine, especially near coincident, polar or antipodal points.

axis_alignment.directed_axis: For a directed unit vector a and target n, psi=acos(a dot n).
axis_alignment.undirected_axis: If +a and -a represent the same geometric axis, use psi_axis=acos(|a dot n|), restricted to 0..pi/2.
axis_alignment.multiple_targets: A candidate undirected axis can be fit by maximizing sum_i w_i (a dot n_i)^2 subject to |a|=1; the solution is the dominant eigenvector of M=sum_i w_i n_i n_i^T.
axis_alignment.interpretation: This supplies an objective best-fit axis for a predeclared target set rather than drawing a line by eye after seeing the data.
axis_alignment.uncertainty: Propagate catalog coordinate uncertainties and any uncertainty in a through Monte Carlo or analytic covariance methods.

null_alignment_probability.single_directed_target: For an isotropically random direction, probability of lying within angular radius psi_0 of a specified directed point is p=(1-cos psi_0)/2.
null_alignment_probability.undirected_axis: For proximity within psi_0<=90 degrees of either pole of a specified undirected axis, p_axis=1-cos psi_0.
null_alignment_probability.multiple_comparisons: If many stars, axes, epochs or tolerances were searched and only the best match reported, the nominal p above is not the experiment-level probability. Search multiplicity must be predeclared or corrected.
null_alignment_probability.project_value: This distinguishes an actually narrow predeclared alignment from a post-hoc visual coincidence.

local_horizon_coordinates.hour_angle: H=local sidereal angle-alpha under the selected conventions
local_horizon_coordinates.requirement: Local azimuth/altitude claims require an explicit observer position and timestamp. Repository or account location should never be silently substituted for a historical observation.
local_horizon_coordinates.project_use: This lets 'look/point north and see X' be tested for a specific event while keeping global equatorial alignment claims separate.

epoch_and_motion.model: n(t_2)=R_frame/precession(t_1->t_2)[n(t_1)+proper-motion update+...] in an appropriate astrometric pipeline
epoch_and_motion.rule: Do not compare a modern horizon direction, J2000 catalog coordinate and ancient/historical pole using raw numbers as though the frame were fixed.
epoch_and_motion.standards: Use IAU/SOFA or equivalent validated astrometry routines for precision precession-nutation and Earth-orientation work.

worked_catalog_sanity_check.purpose: Demonstrate why the project's celestial language needs angular measurement rather than verbal proximity.
worked_catalog_sanity_check.catalog_frame: SIMBAD ICRS coordinates at epoch J2000 as listed in the cited entries; proper motion means apparent catalog positions change with epoch.
worked_catalog_sanity_check.derived: Using the great-circle formula on those J2000 coordinates gives Sirius-Regulus separation approximately 57.83 degrees. Their angular distances from the north celestial pole are approximately 106.72 degrees for Sirius and 78.03 degrees for Regulus because separation from the NCP equals 90 degrees minus declination.
worked_catalog_sanity_check.conclusion: Neither star is collinear with the north celestial pole in this coordinate sense. This does not negate symbolic North/Dog/Lion mappings; it simply prevents physical-axis language from being inferred from symbolism.
worked_catalog_sanity_check.precision_note: These values are sanity-check calculations from catalog coordinates, not a replacement for epoch-corrected astrometry in a historical pointing test.

precession_measurement.dimension_rule: A period [time] and a distance [length] are categorically different even when their numerical values happen to be near 26,000 in chosen units.
precession_measurement.archive_correction: Keep Earth's roughly 25.8-kyr axial-precession timescale separate from the roughly 26-kly Earth-to-Galactic-Center distance. Numeric resemblance is not dimensional equality.
precession_measurement.testable_question: If an Eye/Axis claim depends on a historical epoch, compute the actual pole/target separation at that epoch rather than using the modern pole.

parameters.R: major radius from torus center to tube centerline
parameters.r: minor/tube radius, with R>r for a ring torus

torus_geometry.underdetermination: One remembered length such as 115,000 miles cannot uniquely specify both R and r. Even if it is known to be C_major, it gives R=C/(2pi) but leaves r and therefore area/volume/aspect ratio undetermined.
torus_geometry.recovery_rule: The historic 115,000-mile object should remain unresolved until the original quantity, units, major/minor radius and physical referent are recovered.

coordinate_types_to_keep_separate.equatorial: RA/Dec relative to celestial reference frame
coordinate_types_to_keep_separate.ecliptic: coordinates relative to Earth's orbital plane
coordinate_types_to_keep_separate.galactic: coordinates relative to Milky Way reference plane/center
coordinate_types_to_keep_separate.rule: Any claimed equality or alignment must name the transformation between coordinate types.

research_protocol.step_1: Recover exact wording and date of the celestial claim.
research_protocol.step_2: Classify claim as symbolic, geographic, equatorial, galactic, magnetic or local-horizon.
research_protocol.step_3: Obtain catalog/ephemeris data with uncertainties and epoch.
research_protocol.step_4: Define Axis vector and tolerance before computing match.
research_protocol.step_5: Transform all quantities into one common frame/epoch.
research_protocol.step_7: Evaluate null/multiple-comparison context if statistical significance is claimed.
research_protocol.step_8: Report physical result separately from symbolic interpretation.

conclusions: North becomes scientifically meaningful only after its coordinate type and reference frame are declared.
An Axis can be estimated from target vectors rather than chosen visually, and alignment has a calculable angular residual.
The Sirius/Regulus project motifs are meaningful as documented symbolic/chronological objects but do not by themselves establish astronomical collinearity with terrestrial north.
Precession, proper motion and observer location are not details; they define the measurement.
The remembered torus length is mathematically underdetermined because torus geometry requires at least two independent radii.
